candidato.titulo: Clinical trials generate promising results for improving kidney health
candidato.resumo: The results of numerous high-impact Phase III clinical trials that could affect kidney-related medical care were presented in person at American Society of Nephrology Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

texto_fonte:
Clinical trials generate promising results for improving kidney health
The results of numerous high-impact Phase III clinical trials that could affect kidney-related medical care were presented in person at American Society of Nephrology Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.
Atacicept inhibits the cytokines B-cell activating factor (BAFF, also known as B-lymphocyte stimulator, or BLyS) and a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL) involved in the pathogenesis of IgA nephropathy. In the interim analysis of the Phase III ORIGIN 3 trial, atacicept achieved a statistically significant reduction in urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio at week 36.
Following FDA review, atacicept received accelerated approval. In the latest analysis of ORIGIN 3 through two years, atacicept demonstrated additional benefits for patients.
"ORIGIN 3 stands as a landmark trial in kidney medicine, demonstrating kidney protection with atacicept through stabilization of eGFR and a marked reduction in the risk of kidney disease progression. The safety profile was comparable to placebo, with no evidence of increased infection risk," said corresponding author Jonathan Barratt, MBChB, Ph.D., FRCP, of the University of Leicester.
"Together with a small-volume, self-administered autoinjector, these findings represent an important advance for patients with IgA nephropathy."
Sibeprenlimab targets the cytokine a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL), one of the immune-related drivers of IgA nephropathy, a condition that affects patients often at a young age and places them at a significant lifetime risk of kidney failure. In the Phase III VISIONARY trial, sibeprenlimab reduced the risk of serious kidney function loss or kidney failure in adults with IgA nephropathy by 97% compared with placebo, with kidney function remaining stable over two years.
"By selectively inhibiting APRIL, a fundamental driver of the disease, we are targeting the source of kidney damage and advancing what may be a new standard for treating IgA nephropathy," said corresponding author Dana Rizk, M.D., of the University of Alabama at Birmingham.
Dual inhibition of the cytokines B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS) and a proliferation-inducing ligand (APRIL) targets the underlying pathogenesis of IgA nephropathy.
In a report on the two-year efficacy and safety of the dual BLyS/APRIL inhibitor telitacicept in the Phase III TELIGAN trial, investigators showed that telitacicept slows kidney function loss and substantially reduces the risk of kidney failure in high-risk IgA nephropathy, with a favorable safety profile.
"These two-year findings confirm durable kidney protection for patients with high-risk IgA nephropathy," said corresponding author Jicheng Lv, M.D., Ph.D., of Peking University First Hospital.

candidato.titulo: This ‘living drug’ could change the course of autoimmune disease
candidato.resumo: If given the green light by the FDA, a CAR T cell therapy from Kyverna Therapeutics would be the first approved treatment for stiff person syndrome.

texto_fonte:
Two months before the treatment that would change Lynn Montgomery-Haga’s life, she could barely walk down a hallway.
In a test at the University of Colorado Anschutz, Montgomery-Haga struggled to walk 25 feet, often reaching out to the walls for support. Usually, the 49-year-old relied on her walker or wheelchair. “She had a very stiff, hesitant gait,” says Montgomery-Haga’s neurologist, Amanda Piquet.
For about a decade, Montgomery-Haga had lived with a debilitating autoimmune disease known as stiff person syndrome. The progressive condition can lock up the body’s muscles without warning, leading to falls, broken bones, excruciating pain and difficulty moving. Singer Celine Dion, who returned to the stage in September after years of battling the disease, has said it can feel “like somebody’s strangling you.”
Montgomery-Haga’s own days were marked by dizziness, fatigue and pain. And sudden muscle spasms would send her sprawling. It was like the fainting goat videos popular on the internet, she says. “They get surprised and they fall over, and there’s nothing they can do about it.”
But stiff person syndrome is no joke. It stripped Montgomery-Haga of her accounting job and her ability to drive. She couldn’t sit up in bed unless she had a safety bar to pull on. If she dropped the soap in the shower, it’d take her 10 minutes to pick it up.
Now, Montgomery-Haga hopes those struggles are finally coming to an end. That’s because a clinical trial with an experimental therapy has helped restore mobility for her — and others like her. She can stride through her living room again. She can landscape her front yard. She doesn’t have to brace herself when her dogs jump on her. And she hasn’t fallen once since the treatment. The change has been drastic, she says. “I’m just really excited about the future.”
The treatment, a type of CAR T cell therapy, extracts immune cells from a person’s body and engineers them to attack the very cells causing the disease. First used to fight cancer, CAR T is now also targeting a variety of autoimmune diseases. If given the green light by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Montgomery-Haga’s treatment would be the first such therapy approved for an autoimmune condition — and it would be the first approved treatment for stiff person syndrome.
Stiff person syndrome may be just the beginning, says Carl June, the University of Pennsylvania immunologist and oncologist who spearheaded CAR T cell therapy for cancer decades ago. The “living drug” could herald a new era of therapeutics for autoimmune diseases like lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and even multiple sclerosis. “It’s revolutionary to think how far things have gone,” June says.
But he warns that it’s far too early to know if scientists have definitively cured stiff person syndrome. And there haven’t been enough people treated to get a good handle on all the possible side effects. “There could be long-term complications in autoimmune patients that don’t happen in our cancer patients,” he says. Other researchers urge caution. “It’s very important not to oversell it,” says Marc Scherlinger, a rheumatologist at Strasbourg University Hospital in France.
For Piquet, one crucial question is how long the treatment will last. In Montgomery-Haga’s case, the answer seems to be at least two years. Montgomery-Haga still considers herself disabled, or “disabled-ish,” as she calls it. But when rating how she used to feel on a scale of one to 10, she’d put herself at a zero before treatment, she says. These days, she’s more like a seven.
What’s more, Montgomery-Haga says, “I think I’m still improving.”
No approved therapies
There’s no single symptom that clued Montgomery-Haga in to her disease. In 2014, she started having difficulty picking things up off the floor. Then her boss asked her why she was limping — Montgomery-Haga hadn’t noticed. Her balance was off and her head felt weird, like “I was walking around in a fishbowl,” she says. It got to the point where Montgomery-Haga had difficulty crossing thresholds between rooms.
Montgomery-Haga would startle easily, prompting her body to stiffen up like a board. One time when cooking, she burned her finger, spasmed and collapsed, cracking the back of her head on the cabinets. She lay on the floor crying, but finally managed to right herself. “As soon as you hit the floor,” she says, “your muscles are like, ‘Fine,’ and you can get up again.”
Those unpredictable symptoms capture a slice of what life is like with stiff person syndrome, or SPS. The disease, which affects roughly 2 in 100,000 people in the United States, typically develops in a person’s 30s or 40s. It is about twice as common in women as in men.
Scientists don’t know what sets off the disease. But they think a person’s own antibodies start attacking a neurological network that helps muscles throughout the body relax. And when those tensed muscles are in opposition, like the biceps and triceps, they start fighting one another, Piquet says. That’s when people can end up in a stuck position, leading to stiffness. But because everyone’s immune system is different, patients’ experiences with the disease can vary greatly.
For Tara Zier, a former dentist based in Maryland, SPS started with extreme neck pain, blood pressure spikes, shortness of breath and feelings of impending doom. While some people struggle with mobility, Zier’s difficulties include standing and extreme fatigue. When she holds herself upright, her muscles clamp down on her spine like it’s in a vise. “Have you ever had a charley horse in your calf?” she asks. “Imagine one in your whole body that stops you in your tracks.”
Zier and Montgomery-Haga went years before learning what was behind their symptoms. Their cases mystified doctors — Zier saw 13 specialists and visited the emergency room nine times before getting a diagnosis. When she finally found out she had SPS three years after her first symptoms, Zier says she felt validated, like medicine was confirming what she already knew: “Something’s wrong with me.”
Montgomery-Haga’s 2018 diagnosis put her “over the moon,” she says. For nearly four years, she had gotten sicker and sicker — but doctors couldn’t tell her why. She felt as if they were giving up on her. With the diagnosis, Montgomery-Haga not only learned that SPS existed, she says, “I was told it’s treatable.”
Current treatments include muscle relaxers, anti-seizure medications and Botox injections in body parts that feel especially stiff. Although these off-label therapies can address people’s symptoms, they’re “doing nothing to treat the underlying autoimmune disease,” Piquet says. And some can come with potent side effects, like mental fog.
Zier, who has tried multiple combinations of different meds, remembers frequently losing her train of thought. She has since tapered off all but one drug, a low dose of Valium. “The trade-off,” she says, “is pain.”
People with SPS can also receive intravenous infusions of healthy antibodies, a treatment called IVIG, to decrease muscle spasms and stiffness. Montgomery-Haga found it helpful but time-consuming. She’d go to the clinic every three weeks for an infusion, which could take up to six hours.
“The bottom line is there are no FDA-approved therapies for this disease,” Piquet says. Now, the one most likely to cross the finish line first is something no one would have expected even a few years ago, CAR T pioneer June says. If you told doctors that CAR T cell therapy was going to be FDA approved for an autoimmune disease, he says, “people would have laughed.”
To catch a killer
June may be best known for his work in cancer, but he’s been keenly following the progress in auto-immune therapy. His daughter, now in her 30s, was diagnosed with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis when she was 9 years old. For her, that’s meant over 20 years of treatment with drugs that bring a bundle of side effects, such as fatigue and risk of infections. “It would be much better to be cured,” he says.
In autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and SPS, a person’s own antibodies attack tissues throughout the body, from blood vessels to cartilage to neurons. Wiping out these rogue antibodies can stop the attacks. But CAR T cell therapy doesn’t act on the antibodies themselves. It goes straight to the source, snuffing out the cellular factories that manufacture them.
Those antibody factories are known as B cells. To eliminate them, doctors recruit T cells, which act as the body’s security system and work together to hunt down and destroy problematic cells. In the lab, scientists fine-tune these hunters, outfitting them with a molecular homing device called a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. When infused back into patients’ bodies, the newly-engineered T cells can target the antibody factories directly — like a saboteur told exactly what to destroy.
A new treatment
The CAR T cell therapy Lynn Montgomery-Haga received wipes out B cells, including the ones likely driving her disease. Doctors hope this therapy “resets” her immune system, getting rid of harmful B cells and letting healthy new ones take their place.
“The secret behind CAR T cell therapy is that you completely deplete B cells in the body,” says Georg Schett, a rheumatologist at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg in Germany. Temporarily wiping out a person’s B cells lets the body replace them with fresh, unproblematic ones, Schett says. He calls it an “immune reset.”
CAR T cell therapy got its start in the 2010s, when researchers used engineered T cells to target cancer. In 2017, the FDA approved the first CAR T cell therapies for two blood cancers, acute lymphoblastic leukemia and large B cell lymphoma. Soon after, scientists saw the first tantalizing hints that it might work for autoimmune diseases, too. In some cases, cancer patients with autoimmune disorders reported improvements in both conditions after treatment.
But most researchers didn’t think it could be that easy, Schett says. After all, autoimmune diseases were driven by a complex network of cell types. How could targeting just one of them work?
That thinking underwent a paradigm shift in 2021 when Schett and his team published the first major paper reporting a successful treatment with the therapy. The patient was a 20-year-old woman with a severe case of lupus, a complex, sometimes-fatal illness that can damage the kidneys and other organs. Within five weeks of CAR T cell therapy treatment, signs of her disease began to vanish.
Results like these were “unheard of,” says rheumatologist Maximilian Konig of Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore. Lupus is extremely difficult to treat, and for decades, most drugs tested against it failed. No one had ever seen the kind of improvements that Schett’s patient experienced.
After the paper came out, “everybody was talking about it,” Konig says. Today, more than five years later, the woman’s lupus hasn’t returned, Schett says. “We consider this patient cured,” he says.
The woman’s response was no fluke. The following year, Schett’s team reported similar results in five more lupus patients. All went into remission after CAR T cell therapy.
This was the true tipping point, June says. “It’s rare, very rare, that you get such striking results.”
What followed was an explosion of research around the world. Scientists are now testing CAR T cell therapy in nearly a dozen autoimmune diseases linked to harmful B cells, including lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and a connective-tissue disease known as systemic sclerosis.
Kyverna, the California-based company behind the SPS trial, is also running trials for neurological autoimmune conditions including generalized myasthenia gravis and progressive multiple sclerosis, or MS.
One reason using CAR T cell therapy for neurological conditions excites researchers is because of the cells’ potential to slip past the blood-brain barrier. That means they might be able to access pockets of smoldering inflammation inaccessible to other drugs, says neurologist Rebecca Farber of Columbia University.
That could be a huge help in diseases like MS, in which a person’s antibodies attack the protective sheaths around nerve cells, causing numbness, brain fog and difficulty walking. Still, Farber doubts that CAR T cell therapy could fix existing damage. “We’re not expecting it to repair the nervous system,” she says. But it’s possible the treatment could freeze the disease’s progress. Patients are already asking her team about future treatments.
For Piquet, who cares for roughly 100 people with SPS, Kyverna’s trial offered a compelling opportunity to help her patients. Montgomery-Haga cried when Piquet told her about the trial at one of their regular Zoom appointments. She recalls wondering, is this the treatment that “might help me be normal again?”
The good, the bad and the potentially ugly
Though Montgomery-Haga leapt at the chance to try Kyverna’s treatment, called miv-cel, CAR T cell therapy is no walk in the park. Before starting, doctors sit patients down to “talk about the good, the bad and the potentially ugly,” Piquet says.
That includes the rigorous prep work needed before people receive their engineered T cells. Patients must first get low-dose chemotherapy, which flushes T cells from the body and makes space for the new ones. Chemo can ambush the body with symptoms including hair thinning, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.
Treatment itself also carries risks. It destroys most B cells in the body — not just the ones that cause disease. That can lead to fever, inflammation and potentially risky infections. In Kyverna’s trial, for example, 15 percent of participants had severely low white blood cell counts after treatment. Such symptoms were expected, Piquet says, and were easily treated.
Other CAR T treatments seem to have fared far worse. In August, the pharmaceutical company Novartis paused clinical trials of its therapy, rap-cel, across a spectrum of autoimmune diseases after three patients died. Bristol Myers Squibb has also paused similar studies after some patients experienced neurological complications, according to the Wall Street Journal. Details of the incidents were slow to emerge and have set the field on edge. “It’s a tragedy,” Konig says. He calls such outcomes an important wake-up call.
But red flags in one trial don’t mean all CAR T products are dangerous, Konig says. That’s because many different designs and manufacturing processes exist, and scientists can’t always predict what will make one product toxic and another safe. Kyverna’s miv-cel, for instance, has been consistently well-tolerated in the more than 100 patients treated, a spokesperson for the company says.
CAR T cell therapies are transformative, Konig says. “They’re going to change the field — but there are risks.”
Another risk is that the once-vanquished disease will return. Doctors don’t know all the genetic and environmental conditions that trigger autoimmune disease. Some researchers wonder whether vulnerable individuals remain vulnerable, even after treatment. But because it often takes multiple insults for someone to tip into a state of disease, Scherlinger says, CAR T cell therapy could buy patients lots of time.
“Now I can”
After 10 days in the hospital for her treatment, Montgomery-Haga returned to recover at home. In the following months, she started to notice some changes. It was easier getting around the house, for one. And she felt her balance and stability improving. She can now kneel down to garden and clean without the days of recovery it used to require. “I can vacuum my house,” she says. “It seems so little, but now I can vacuum!”
Montgomery-Haga can even sit down “crisscross applesauce,” she says. “I couldn’t do that for, like, 10 years.”
Four months after the treatment, Piquet’s team tested Montgomery-Haga’s walking ability. In a hallway at University of Colorado Anschutz’s research building, the team marked out 25 feet with little orange cones. At one end stood Montgomery-Haga. At the other, Piquet watched behind a video camera. This time, Montgomery-Haga’s gait was smooth and her arms were down, not hovering out into the air to catch herself if she fell. “You could see that she was walking with a lot more confidence,” Piquet says.
The team saw similar results in other SPS patients. Some who had difficulty walking before treatment now wanted to run, Piquet says. “It’s incredible to just see those patients speeding down the hallway.” She remembers smiles, high fives and a sense of celebration in the air. Eight of 12 people who had used a walking aid for the initial test didn’t need one for the follow-up, Piquet reported at the American Academy of Neurology meeting in April.
In September, Kyverna reported the trial’s one-year results: Patients maintained mobility improvements, with a third completing their 25-foot walk about as fast as a healthy adult. Additionally, nearly all patients no longer rely on immuno-suppressive drugs to tamp down harmful immune activity. That’s good news because such drugs can bring all sorts of nasty side effects, like vomiting, bleeding and infections.
The results with SPS are “really something to celebrate,” June says. But only time and many more treatments will reveal how safe CAR T really is, he says.
That’s a concern for Zier, who says she wouldn’t feel comfortable trying the therapy at this point. Zier doesn’t know how she’d respond. She’s a single mother with two kids; even a rare side effect could disrupt her life in a way she may not be able to manage. And these days, she’s managing as well as she can. Zier is the founder and CEO of The Stiff Person Syndrome Research Foundation, which supports research for SPS treatments.
Kyverna is in the process of submitting miv-cel for FDA approval. The company is seeking priority review and hopes the treatment might be available to patients in 2027. If SPS is the first autoimmune disease to have an FDA-approved CAR T cell therapy, myasthenia gravis could be the second, says Warner Biddle, Kyverna’s CEO. What’s more, miv-cel also appeared to improve symptoms in six patients with severe cases of rheumatoid arthritis, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.
As for what’s next, the door is wide open. Some scientists are working to make off-the-shelf forms of CAR T that wouldn’t require personalized engineering. Others are trying to reprogram T cells directly inside people’s bodies, rather than in the lab. Still others are trying to make T cells that target only the B cells responsible for disease. In the future, doctors might use such drugs to help patients avoid the cumbersome treatment process that Montgomery-Haga endured.
Montgomery-Haga’s own future looks far different than what she had imagined a few years ago. In 2026, she took a trip to Washington, D.C., to see the monuments. Now she’d like to visit Paris, Scotland and Ireland, too.
For so many years, Montgomery-Haga has looked at trips and activities — and even household chores — that most people take for granted, thinking, “Man, I wish I could do that,” she says. “Now I can.”

candidato.titulo: Dream Labs raises $90M and launches Dream API
candidato.resumo: Dream Labs says its Dream-1 AI model works across robots from different manufacturers and will allow robots to transfer their learning. The post Dream Labs raises $90M and launches Dream API appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
More brains are coming for robots. Dream Labs this week said it has raised $90 million in seed funding. The company also launched Dream API, a publicly available application programming interface to turn a robot’s camera feed and a plain-English instructions into motor commands, even for robots it has never seen before.
Factories worldwide run a record 5 million industrial robots, yet nearly every one is programmed for a single task, and most cannot transfer what they have learned to other machines, noted Dream Labs. Low-cost robots now sell for a few thousand dollars but ship with no built-in intelligence. Teaching one robot one task can take specialists months, and a new task or new hardware often means starting from zero, according to the San Francisco startup.
Dream Labs said its Dream-1 flagship model works across robots from different manufacturers. Trained on video of people performing everyday tasks, it can predict what will happen next and determine the robot’s resulting action. Because it learns from video rather than from a single machine, its capabilities transfer across hardware, Dream Labs claimed.
The company said Dream-1 can control any robot “out of the box” with grippers and zero-shot learning.
“The hardware is ready. What’s been missing is a brain any robot can use,” stated Joel Jang, co-founder and CEO of Dream Labs. “When you get into a rental car, you don’t relearn how to drive. You find the controls, and your past driving experience does the rest.”
“Dream-1 approaches a new robot the same way, so a new robot can do useful work in minutes, not months,” he added. “And instead of edited demos, we’re giving people a working model they can test themselves, mistakes included.”
B Capital and Kindred Ventures led the round. It also included participation from A.Capital, Unusual Ventures, SV Angel, Wing VC, Scribble VC, and Adrian Aoun, among others.
Inside Dream Labs’ product portfolio
Developers and robot enthusiasts can start using Dream Labs’ AI products today. The company said Dream API translates visual inputs and natural language prompts directly into robot actions.
Developers can sign up, connect any robots with grippers, and the robot will carry out the task. Dream Labs runs its models in data centers around the world, so robots respond quickly wherever they are.
The company also offers fine-tuning as a service. For unsupported hardware or new capabilities, developers and robot makers can submit a small batch of demonstration data to receive a tailored model within hours.
Developers also have access to Dream Labs’ robot playground. Anyone with a browser can type commands to a robot in Dream Labs’ San Francisco office and watch it respond live and unedited, no robot purchase required.
“A capable robot arm has gone from the price of a luxury car to the price of a high-end laptop. What it needs now is intelligence,” said Daisy Cai, general partner at B Capital. “This team did some of the defining work in robot learning at NVIDIA. Now anyone with an API key can build on it.”
Startup works with more than 20 hardware partners
Dream Labs supports robots today that cost between about $2,000 and $10,000. Dream-1 needs no extra data to control a two-armed robot with parallel grippers.
For its over 20 hardware partners, Dream Labs said it goes beyond that baseline, refining the model for each robot so it performs at its best. Dream-1 currently handles tabletop tasks such as picking and placing objects and folding laundry, with support for wheeled mobile robots and dexterous hands to follow.
The company said it plans use the new funding primarily for compute as it expands the tasks and robots Dream-1 can handle, and scales to support more users.
“Our customers buy our robots to build things, and the hardest part has always been getting them to do actual work,” said Ryan Chan, co-founder and CEO of MakerMods, which sells $2,000 bimanual robot arms. “With Dream-1, our robot was up and running in a few minutes and attempting tasks we never programmed. We can focus on building better hardware, and our customers get intelligence that keeps improving.”

candidato.titulo: Estudantes de Pedagogia organizam debates para o Mês da Consciência Negra
candidato.resumo: Educação antirracista, racialização e luta quilombola integram a programação aberta à comunidade, nos dias 23 e outubro, 11 e 19 de novembro

texto_fonte:
Por Sofhia Camargo*
O curso de Pedagogia da Faculdade de Filosofia, Ciências e Letras de Ribeirão Preto (FFCLRP) da USP promove uma série de eventos no Mês da Consciência Negra. As atividades serão nos dias 23 de outubro, 11 e 19 de novembro, a partir das 19h, e é voltado à comunidade USP e externa. Os interessados devem fazer a inscrição pelos formulários disponíveis no perfil do Instagram oficial do curso neste link, que serão disponibilizados conforme a aproximação da data das palestras.
Organizado por alunos do curso, com a premissa de permitir a maior participação de estudantes e da comunidade e com isso ampliar os debates sobre as relações étnico-raciais, a educação antirracista e as lutas históricas da população negra, a iniciativa conta conferências e intervenções artísticas.
Os temas selecionados para cada dia são: Saberes necessários à educação para as relações étnico-raciais, com a professora Petronilha Beatriz Gonçalves; Racialização e política: possibilidades e limites da educação, com o professor Leonardo Freitas Sacramento da Rede Municipal de Educação de Ribeirão Preto e Instituto Federal de Sertãozinho; Comunidade Quilombola dos Jerônimos: resistência e luta ancestral, com a professora Yara de Cássia Alves e a Yalorixá Simone Souza.
No último dia, o Bloco Guardiões do N´Goma fará uma apresentação musical e, além da parte artística, pretende apresentar para o público a importância da experiência, luta, conhecimento, trabalho e resistência das comunidades quilombolas para a preservação de territórios e culturas.
Mais informações: perfis do Instagram pedagousprp e cepedusp.
*Estagiária sob supervisão de Rose Talamone

candidato.titulo: TSMC is seeking chipmaking equipment that doesn't contain Chinese rare-earth magnets
candidato.resumo: TSMC is reportedly asking equipment suppliers for factory machinery that doesn't use rare-earth components, as the chipmaker seeks to reduce exposure to China’s dominance of critical minerals and permanent magnets.

texto_fonte:
TSMC, the world's largest contract chip manufacturer, is seeking alternative machinery without rare-earth components to reduce its dependence on China-dominated materials and avoid disruptions to factory operations caused by the country's export controls. According to a Reuters report on October 22 citing people familiar with the matter, the Taiwanese company has begun approaching its equipment suppliers to explore whether they can provide factory automation equipment equipped with motors that don't require rare-earth materials.
TSMC supplies the extremely powerful Nvidia chips that are facilitating the AI boom. It also manufactures chips for Apple, Broadcom, Qualcomm, and numerous other tech and automotive companies. The company operates enormous, highly automated semiconductor fabrication plants. These factories use industrial machinery that relies on electric motors with powerful permanent magnets made from rare-earth elements such as neodymium, dysprosium, and terbium.
According to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), China accounts for roughly 70% of global rare earth mining. The International Energy Agency (IEA) says China also controls around 90% of refining and approximately 95% of the finished permanent magnets found in TSMC’s machines, giving Beijing a quasi-absolute monopoly over one of the most critical technology supply chains. In April 2025, the country placed seven medium and heavy rare earths and the magnets made from them under export controls, requiring exporters to seek case-by-case approval and export licenses, thereby choking shipments to manufacturers across the U.S., Europe, and Asia, including TSMC.
China expanded the controls on October 9, 2025, to include five additional rare earths, processing technology and equipment, and even products manufactured outside the country that contain more than 0.1% Chinese-origin rare earths, or are made using Chinese processing technology. It later suspended the October expansion for one year, until November 10, 2026. This has now been extended for an additional 90 days.
TSMC’s moves aim to reduce the risk that these controls will hinder production at its factories. Even with all other raw materials and machinery required to manufacture its chips, shortages of specialized motor components could complicate the maintenance, repair, or expansion of its production equipment. Several technological approaches allow motors to avoid rare earth magnets. Conventional induction motors, for example, generate torque using electromagnetic induction rather than permanent magnets. Switched-reluctance motors are another option, while some permanent-magnet motors can use ferrite magnets instead of rare-earth magnets. However, these technologies typically involve different trade-offs in efficiency, size, power density, precision, and control requirements.
Meanwhile, the rest of the world is undertaking the painstaking, drawn-out task of building a rare-earth supply chain outside China. Taiwan is reportedly pursuing domestic rare-earth production capabilities in collaboration with the United States, with both countries confirming their intent to reduce reliance on Chinese rare-earth and critical-mineral supply chains.
Taiwan's government is supporting the Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) in establishing a pilot production line within three years that could supply about 50% of Taiwan's domestic rare-earth demand. Meanwhile, the U.S. is “working with Taiwan and other partners to develop alternative sources of supply, expand processing capacity and build more resilient supply chains,” according to the report. In February 2026, the Trump administration announced plans to create a $12 billion critical minerals stockpile to offset supply chain risks from China.

candidato.titulo: Stars brewing in a nebulous cauldron
candidato.resumo: Image: Stars brewing in a nebulous cauldron

texto_fonte:
In this Picture of the Month from the NASA/ESA James Webb Space Telescope, we visit a turbulent cauldron of star formation to see what is brewing inside dense clumps of gas. This is a star-forming region named LHA 120-N 159, or simply N159, located 161 000 light-years away in the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC), one of the satellite galaxies orbiting the Milky Way galaxy. This image spans about 230 light-years across.
N159 is what astronomers call a light-years: an area of space filled with ionised hydrogen gas. In stellar nurseries such as this one, giant molecular clouds of cold hydrogen gas collapse under gravity, forming new stars. Many of these stars are extremely massive and hot, and their powerful ultraviolet radiation ionises the gas around them. This makes H II regions markers of active star formation, and as the ionised gas radiates light this turns them into the kind of brilliant emission nebula that we see in this image. The fierce stellar winds from these stars sculpt dense ridges and carve open cavities in the gas, which Webb’s Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) captures here in great detail.
The roiling brew of star formation in N159 is closed in by thick, smoky orange clouds that also billow across the centre of the image. The light orange colour signifies light emitted by polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, an important carbon-based molecule. The pools of pale blue gas are clouds of H II gas, ionised by the intense ultraviolet light from massive stars. Dark red filaments cross the centre of the image, particularly visible above the blue region on the right side; these are made of cool molecular hydrogen. These filaments are the densest part of the nebula and currently shield new stars from harsh radiation and stellar winds – by zooming in, you can see stars as points of light embedded in these filaments and in the small pillars of orange gas that reach out into the blue bubbles. Eventually, these structures will melt away, leaving their completed stars behind.
The LMC is full of H II regions like N159 conveniently located for us to study, including the larger N79 region and the spectacular Tarantula Nebula. They are not exactly like the star-forming regions within our own galaxy: the LMC’s metallicity – its proportion of the elements, which astronomers call 'metals', that are heavier than hydrogen and helium – is significantly lower than in the Milky Way galaxy. This gives researchers an opportunity to study H II regions in conditions that are more similar to those found in the early Universe, helping us to learn about star formation in that time.
At less than three million years old, N159 is one of the youngest star-forming regions of the LMC, containing thousands of stars at their earliest stages of formation. Since the advent of space telescopes astronomers have closely examined the stellar populations in N159. The brightly glowing spot on the left side of the image is the Papillon Nebula, an exceptionally compact blob of ionised hydrogen that is thought to be linked to the formation of massive stars: it was resolved for the first time by the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope in 1999. Sections of the sweeping clouds of gas were featured in a pair of images from Hubble in 2025, covering east and west sides of the cloud.
The data used in this new Webb image come from an observing programme (#5114) aiming to study and compare stars throughout their different stages of evolution in this giant nebula. In the resulting paper, astronomers delved into N159 with greater detail thanks to these new and comprehensive Webb data. They were able to detect extremely dim stars less than a tenth as massive as the Sun, and distinguish larger, hotter, fully evolved stars from the young stellar objects still wrapped up in the thick clouds where they are born. Their results showed that the western region of N159 has more of these young stellar objects in a more concentrated area, showing that it is at an earlier stage of collapsing to form stars. With the whole sequence of star formation taking place at once, N159 is a unique place to see the evolution of a collapsing molecular cloud up close.
[Image Description: A nebula made of clouds of gas and dust with stars forming within. In the centre and out to the left it is filled with thin, wispy blue gas that forms delicate layers. Around this are thicker orange clouds with dark ridges. Thin red filaments of gas cross the centre of the nebula. Glowing bubbles in the gas contain dense, very bright clusters of stars. In the edges, distant stars are visible as bright points on a dark background.]

candidato.titulo: Lost Schrödinger manuscript reveals his true view of quantum randomness
candidato.resumo: Unlike classical physics, quantum mechanics generally cannot tell us exactly what will happen in an individual event. Instead, it predicts the probabilities of different outcomes. As one of the theory's early pioneers, Erwin Schrödinger played a key role in debates about what this randomness really means. However, part of his contribution has stayed hidden for more than 80 years.

texto_fonte:
Lost Schrödinger manuscript reveals his true view of quantum randomness
Sam Jarman
Author
Unlike classical physics, quantum mechanics generally cannot tell us exactly what will happen in an individual event. Instead, it predicts the probabilities of different outcomes. As one of the theory's early pioneers, Erwin Schrödinger played a key role in debates about what this randomness really means. However, part of his contribution has stayed hidden for more than 80 years.
In a new study posted on the arXiv preprint server, Flavio Del Santo at the University of Geneva has analyzed an unpublished manuscript by Schrödinger, shedding new light on his thinking.
The determinism debate
In a classical event like a coin toss, the result only seems random because we can't measure every force acting on it. Since the early days of quantum mechanics, some physicists have wondered whether quantum randomness works the same way.
In these 'hidden-variable' theories, particles carry unobserved properties that secretly determine the outcome of each measurement. In 1932, however, mathematician John von Neumann published what many took as proof that such properties couldn't exist, and the idea was largely abandoned.
The question resurfaced in the following decade. In 1943, Edmund Taylor Whittaker argued that quantum mechanics had destroyed the classical idea of a predictable universe. To make his case, he imagined particles of light passing through a polarizer: a filter whose orientation determines how much light gets through.
If each particle carried a hidden instruction to pass or be blocked, Whittaker reasoned that rotating the filter after the light had already set off toward it couldn't change these instructions. In contrast, quantum mechanics predicts that the fraction passing through should change.
After Satyendra Nath Bose made a similar case in 1944, the question sparked a lively debate in the journal Nature. Among the responses, Heinrich Pelzer presented a model showing that Whittaker's argument didn't hold up.
Revisiting Schrödinger's manuscript
Although he is often portrayed as a champion of determinism, Schrödinger himself joined the debate. In a three-page, handwritten response, he built his own hidden-variable model, simply to show that such explanations couldn't be ruled out. Crucially, this didn't mean he believed in a fully predetermined universe. As he put it, experiments and logic could never prove either view impossible.
Surprisingly, however, Schrödinger's manuscript never made it to print. Instead, it has sat largely unnoticed in the Schrödinger archive at the University of Vienna. But in his latest study, Del Santo transcribed the work for the first time, using it to reconstruct the debate from other publications from the time.
Rather than the simple 'yes-or-no' instruction Whittaker had assumed, Schrödinger gave each particle of light a hidden property with a whole range of possible values. Del Santo's calculations confirmed that this model matched the predictions of quantum mechanics—and, going a step beyond Pelzer, it still worked when the same light passed through several filters in a row.
Rethinking Schrödinger's contribution
The analysis dates the manuscript to sometime after November 1944 and suggests Schrödinger may have shelved it after learning of Pelzer's work. More importantly, it paints a more nuanced picture of the physicist.
Since the 1920s, before quantum mechanics had even emerged, Schrödinger had suspected that nature's laws might be fundamentally statistical. Ultimately, Del Santo concludes that his model was a proof of principle, rather than evidence of his commitment to determinism.

You'll get an ad-free account as a thank-you.

texto_fonte:
It’s no longer enough for AI agents to browse the web and check your email; now, they want to sign into your accounts too, and one of the most popular password managers is ready to help out.
1Password has just announced a new feature that allows AI agents like ChatGPT Dots, the just-unveiled Claude Duet, Grok Bot, Meta Muse, and more to tap into your vault of stored usernames and passwords, but without actually seeing them.
Available now for 1Password individual and family accounts, the 1Password for Agents integration lets your supported AI agent log into a website using your 1Password credentials. The agent must first verify its identity with 1Password using a unique digital key; once that’s done, 1Password takes over, plugging your username and password directly into the site without your agent getting to see them.
If this kind of 1Password functionality sounds familiar, you may be thinking of 1Password for Claude, a Claude extension that lets Claude Cowork log into websites using your 1Password credentials without seeing your usernames or passwords.
In an email, 1Password business chief John Torrey told me that 1Password for Agents “builds on integrations like 1Password for Claude,” allowing personal AI agents that aren’t tied to your desktop to securely handle your 1Password credentials.
Torrey stressed that 1Password users will remain in control when it comes to determining when and how agents use their passwords. “The user is involved in every decision,” Torrey said. “Our customers decide which credentials an agent can use and for which task, and for how long. The agent can’t approve its own access.”
At launch, 1Password for Agents will offer integrations for ChatGPT Work and “dot” agents, Claude Duet (the new “proactive” Claude agent), Grok Bot, Meta Muse, and Townie agents.
Noticeably absent from the list is Google’s Gemini Spark agent, as well as Microsoft Scout, but 1Password’s press release notes there are “additional integrations to come.”
I haven’t had a change to try 1Password for Agents yet, but I did try 1Password for Claude upon its release this past summer. It worked as advertised, allowing Claude Cowork to log into my FreshDirect account and go grocery shopping for me, even checking out when it was done.
But while 1Password integrations can now allow AI agents to log into your accounts without seeing your 1Password credentials, what those agents do once they get into your accounts is up to you — and up to them, too.
I felt comfortable letting Claude buy groceries for me (especially since I could check its work and make changes before the delivery date). But would I give Claude access to my bank account or MyChart with 1Password? Not so much.

texto_fonte:
Anthropic lança Claude Duet, IA que cuida de tarefas e e-mails enquanto você dorme
Por Marcelo Fischer |
A Anthropic anunciou, na quarta-feira (21), o Claude Duet, um novo aplicativo de inteligência artificial (IA) capaz de executar tarefas, organizar e-mails e acompanhar compromissos mesmo enquanto o usuário dorme. A ferramenta funciona como um assistente pessoal que toma iniciativas sem precisar receber comandos a todo momento.
Disponível para Android, iOS e pela web, o Duet utiliza o modelo Claude Opus 5.5 e foi desenvolvido principalmente para profissionais e pequenos empresários. A novidade chega para competir com agentes de IA como o Muse, da Meta, e o Dots, da OpenAI.
O lançamento, porém, ainda é limitado. Inicialmente, apenas assinantes dos planos Pro e Max do Claude nos Estados Unidos poderão testar a ferramenta, mediante inscrição em uma lista de espera.
Como funciona o Claude Duet?
O Duet funciona como um agente de IA, tecnologia capaz de executar ações em nome do usuário, incluindo atividades que exigem várias etapas e o uso de diferentes aplicativos.
Para isso, a ferramenta utiliza um computador virtual na nuvem, equipado com um navegador próprio. Dessa forma, consegue continuar trabalhando mesmo quando o usuário fecha o aplicativo ou desliga o celular e o computador.
Segundo a Anthropic, o assistente também aproveita a memória e as integrações já configuradas na conta do Claude. São mais de 6 mil conectores e plugins disponíveis no catálogo da empresa, incluindo serviços como Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar e Google Drive.
Entre as atividades que o Duet pode realizar estão:
- Organizar e-mails: identificar mensagens importantes, preparar respostas e acompanhar conversas sem retorno;
- Gerenciar compromissos: conferir a agenda, identificar conflitos de horários e ajudar no agendamento de reuniões;
- Preparar relatórios: reunir informações de diferentes fontes, produzir pesquisas e criar apresentações;
- Executar tarefas profissionais: elaborar projeções financeiras, acompanhar pagamentos pendentes e desenvolver aplicativos;
- Realizar compras: utilizar serviços de pagamento compatíveis, como Link e Shop Pay, mediante autorização do usuário.
Outro recurso é o resumo matinal. A IA analisa informações dos serviços conectados e apresenta os assuntos que considera mais importantes para o dia, além de sugerir providências.
O usuário também pode conversar com o Duet por texto ou voz, acompanhar tarefas em andamento e receber notificações quando alguma atividade exigir sua participação.
Apesar da proposta de funcionamento contínuo, a Anthropic explica que o aplicativo verifica os serviços conectados em intervalos de algumas horas. Isso evita que o acompanhamento consuma rapidamente os limites de utilização dos planos.
Claude Duet é parecido com o Muse e o Dots?
Sim. Os três aplicativos seguem a proposta de agentes de IA que trabalham de maneira proativa e conseguem executar atividades mesmo quando o usuário está ausente.
O Muse, lançado pela Meta em setembro, é voltado principalmente para atividades pessoais. Ele pode reservar viagens, realizar compras, preencher formulários e até negociar em nome do usuário, dependendo das permissões concedidas.
Já o Dots, apresentado pela OpenAI também em setembro, tem maior foco na continuidade de projetos e tarefas. Integrado ao ChatGPT, o agente consegue trabalhar com outros aplicativos, acompanhar mudanças e apresentar resultados para revisão, inclusive por meio do Slack e do Microsoft Teams.
O Claude Duet se aproxima dos dois concorrentes, mas dá maior destaque à organização da rotina profissional, ao gerenciamento de e-mails e à preparação de documentos.
Há também diferenças na forma de acesso. Enquanto o Dots funciona dentro do ecossistema do ChatGPT, o Claude Duet possui um aplicativo independente. O Muse, por sua vez, pode ser utilizado pelo próprio aplicativo ou pelo WhatsApp.
Quais são os limites e riscos da ferramenta?
A Anthropic afirma que o Duet exige autorização antes de realizar ações consideradas sensíveis, como enviar mensagens, concluir pagamentos, assinar documentos ou excluir informações.
Além disso, determinadas operações são bloqueadas mesmo com a permissão do usuário, incluindo negociações de ações e transferências de dinheiro entre contas.
A empresa também implementou mecanismos para tentar impedir o vazamento de informações confidenciais e ataques conhecidos como prompt injection, nos quais instruções maliciosas escondidas em páginas ou mensagens tentam manipular o comportamento da IA.
Essas proteções, contudo, não eliminam o risco de erros. A própria Anthropic reconhece que o Duet pode interpretar conversas incorretamente, avaliar mal a urgência de compromissos e apresentar dificuldades em tarefas pessoais, como reservar ingressos.
Por enquanto, o sistema também não permite que o usuário visualize diretamente o navegador utilizado pelo agente, o que limita o acompanhamento de determinadas atividades.
Claude Duet está disponível no Brasil?
Ainda não. Segundo a documentação oficial da Anthropic, a versão experimental do Claude Duet está restrita aos Estados Unidos e exige uma conta americana do Claude, assinatura Pro ou Max e convite da lista de espera.
Durante os testes, o aplicativo não terá cobrança adicional para esses assinantes. Entretanto, todas as atividades, inclusive verificações automáticas e tarefas executadas em segundo plano, consomem os limites de uso do plano contratado.
Os planos Team e Enterprise também ficaram de fora do lançamento inicial, embora a Anthropic pretenda ampliar o acesso futuramente.
Não há previsão anunciada para a chegada do Claude Duet ao Brasil. A empresa também não informou quando pretende disponibilizar o aplicativo para usuários gratuitos.

texto_fonte:
VAIO FE16 estreia no Brasil como AI PC "barato" em momento de crise; conheça
Por Raphael Giannotti |
A VAIO anunciou oficialmente a chegada da nova geração do VAIO FE16 ao mercado brasileiro, ampliando o seu portfólio de AI PCs. Fabricado no país pela Positivo Tecnologia desde 2015, o portátil de 16 polegadas é equipado com os novos processadores Intel Wildcat Lake e conta com uma NPU dedicada, com capacidade de até 17 TOPS, para o processamento local de tarefas de inteligência artificial. O modelo já está à venda com preço a partir de R$ 4.999.
O foco do lançamento é democratizar o acesso à inteligência artificial integrada sem restringir o recurso aos modelos premium, embora com uma capacidade inferior. A presença da NPU permite aplicar efeitos de câmera e de áudio em tempo real durante videoconferências, diretamente no dispositivo, economizando bateria e reduzindo a dependência da nuvem. O modelo também vem pronto para o Copilot, contando inclusive com uma tecla dedicada no teclado para acionar o assistente digital.
Design ergonômico e foco em produtividade
A tela de 16 polegadas adota a proporção 16:10 com resolução WUXGA (1920 x 1200) e painel IPS antirreflexo, entregando 11% a mais de área vertical em relação ao padrão 16:9 tradicional. O chassi possui abertura de até 180 graus, espessura de 19,8 mm e peso de 1,8 kg. A estrutura abriga uma bateria de 55 Wh com autonomia estimada em até 10 horas de uso e um sistema de refrigeração com dois heatpipes para manter a estabilidade térmica.
Outro ponto forte do VAIO FE16 é a capacidade de expansão. Diferente de ultrabooks com componentes totalmente soldados, o notebook permite upgrades de memória RAM até 64 GB em padrão DDR5 e armazenamento via SSD NVMe M.2 até 4 TB, garantindo maior vida útil ao PC portátil.
Especificações técnicas do VAIO FE16
- Tela: 16 polegadas IPS, 1920 x 1200, formato 16:10, antirreflexo e abertura até 180°
- Processador: Intel Core Série 3 (Wildcat Lake) com NPU dedicada de até 17 TOPs
- Gráficos: Intel Graphics integrada
- Memória RAM: DDR5 com suporte a expansão até 64 GB
- Armazenamento: SSD NVMe M.2 com suporte até 4 TB
- Bateria: 55 Wh Smart com autonomia de até 10 horas
- Conectividade: Wi-Fi 6 (AX), Bluetooth 5.2 e porta de rede RJ-45 Gigabit
- Portas: 3x USB 3.2 Gen 1, 1x USB Type-C 3.2 Gen 1, 1x HDMI 2.0b (4K a 60 Hz) e leitor de cartão SD
- Teclado: ABNT2 ergonômico, resistente a derramamento de água e com tecla dedicada ao Microsoft Copilot
- Dimensões e Peso: 359 x 255,3 x 19,8 mm; 1,8 kg
E falando no ecossistema da Positivo, a fabricante brasileira lançou, meses atrás, a linha Master Copilot+ com processadores Intel Core Ultra 300 (Panther Lake), oferecendo até 64 GB de memória e 1 TB de SSD.

candidato.resumo: Hackers ligados à Rússia usaram a rede descentralizada Yggdrasil para ocultar comunicações em ataque que destruiu dados na Ucrânia O post Phishing por e-mail abre caminho para ataque destrutivo na Ucrânia apareceu primeiro em Olhar Digital .

texto_fonte:
Hackers ligados à Rússia usaram a rede descentralizada Yggdrasil para ocultar comunicações durante um ataque contra uma empresa ucraniana de logística de grãos. Segundo a ESET, foi o primeiro uso documentado dessa tecnologia por um grupo de hackers ligado a um Estado.
A invasão ocorreu em julho de 2025 e terminou com a destruição de dados nos computadores afetados. Antes da guerra, a agricultura respondia por cerca de um quinto da economia ucraniana e quase metade das exportações do país.
Rede descentralizada dificultou a detecção
A ESET rastreou a invasão até um e-mail de phishing enviado durante uma campanha contra empresas de logística, companhias de grãos e terminais portuários na Ucrânia. Após obter acesso à rede, os invasores instalaram um programa que permitia controlar computadores remotamente, consultar arquivos, fazer capturas de tela e roubar documentos.
A comunicação do programa passava por um servidor escondido na Yggdrasil, uma rede experimental mantida por voluntários e sem proprietário central. Sua estrutura em malha dificulta a detecção das comunicações, segundo a explicação do pesquisador Anton Cherepanov, da ESET.
“Por ser uma rede em malha, é mais difícil de detectar”, afirmou Cherepanov. A empresa disse que não havia observado anteriormente ataques ligados a Estados que utilizassem essa tecnologia.
Ferramenta legítima foi usada para apagar dados
Depois de obter privilégios de administrador, os invasores acionaram o SDelete, utilitário legítimo da Microsoft desenvolvido para apagar arquivos permanentemente.
“Eles abusaram dessa ferramenta legítima”, disse Cherepanov.
A investigação atribuiu a invasão inicial ao UAC-0099, grupo ligado à Rússia especializado em obter acesso a redes. A etapa de destruição de dados apresentou características associadas ao Sandworm, grupo amplamente ligado à inteligência militar russa e anteriormente responsabilizado por ataques contra infraestruturas de energia da Ucrânia e da Polônia.
Segundo a avaliação da ESET, o UAC-0099 conseguiu entrar na rede e transferiu o acesso ao Sandworm. A empresa, porém, não conseguiu determinar qual dos grupos operou a porta dos fundos usada entre a invasão e a destruição dos dados.
A investigação identificou três pontos centrais:
- Invasão inicial: o UAC-0099 foi apontado como responsável pela entrada na rede.
- Transferência de acesso: a ESET avalia que o acesso foi repassado ao Sandworm.
- Autoria ainda indefinida: não foi possível identificar qual grupo operou a porta dos fundos antes da destruição dos dados.
A ESET não divulgou o nome da empresa atingida nem confirmou se o ataque interrompeu suas operações. A Microsoft não respondeu imediatamente ao pedido de comentário.
